title: Learned Routing of Latent State Between LLM Agents
kicker: Doctoral Research Direction · Multi-Agent Language Models
tools: PyTorch · Hugging Face Transformers · vLLM · Qwen3 / Qwen3.5 · Slurm on the OSU (Oregon State University) cluster · W&B (Weights & Biases)
blurb: Can language-model agents share internal state instead of text, and can a manager learn who should read what? A controlled audit of KV-cache (key-value cache) hand-offs found the content does cross, but on standard benchmarks it adds nothing over one agent; when the receiver lacks the facts, the latent channel matches text (91% vs 92%).
long: Teams of LLM (large language model) agents usually talk in text: a worker writes its findings out token by token and every reader re-reads them. Agents built on the same model can instead hand over internal state, such as the KV (key-value) cache of attention. My proposal, written for the NSF GRFP (National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellowship Program), puts a manager in charge of that traffic: workers write compact latent summaries, and the manager learns from team reward which summaries each worker should read under a bandwidth budget, in teams of 8-16 agents.

First, an audit of what actually crosses. I reproduced LatentMAS (a published latent multi-agent method) on Qwen3-4B with GSM8K (grade-school math) and ARC-Challenge (science questions), 300 questions × 3 seeds each, after checking that my implementation gives bit-identical caches and solver logits to the official code. Then I added cache-content controls: a cache built for a different question, no cache, a noise cache, and a sweep over the number of latent steps.

The result is a mixed one, reported as such. The latent team ties a single agent (+0.1 and −0.2 points, 95% intervals spanning zero), while a text team gains 3.4 and 2.4 points. Yet swapping in another question's cache costs 4.0 and 6.2 points, and on GSM8K 16% of the swapped arm's errors are the other question's answer. So content does cross the channel; it just does not help when the receiver can solve the task alone.

Second, a split-information probe where communication is necessary: the sender holds a GSM8K problem's facts and the solver only its question (100 questions, one seed). The right cache scores 91%, a wrong cache or no cache 0%, and a text message 92% (difference −1.0 points, 95% interval −7 to +5). The latent sender needs 2.4× fewer estimated FLOPs (floating-point operations) per question in total and, at batch size 1, 19× less sender time than a text sender that thinks before writing. But its message is 25 MiB of KV cache against 111 text tokens, about 61,000× more bytes, so this measures context sharing, not compression. That gap is what the learned compact summaries in the proposal are meant to close.

Around this sits the infrastructure the plan needs: a harness that runs agents in multi-turn GEM environments and logs every turn to a live viewer, and an RL (reinforcement learning) pipeline, GRPO (group-relative policy optimization) with LoRA (low-rank adaptation), on SWE-smith bug-fixing tasks in network-isolated containers. On 59 held-out tasks × 2, Qwen3.5-4B resolves 54% (64/118) and Qwen3.5-2B 16.9% (20/118). A paper draft on the audit is in progress.
highlights: LatentMAS (latent multi-agent system) reproduction on Qwen3-4B, bit-identical to the official code
Latent team ties a single agent: +0.1 / −0.2 points
Wrong cache costs 4.0 / 6.2 points: content does cross
Split probe: right cache 91%, text 92%, wrong or no cache 0%
Latent sender 19× faster, 2.4× fewer total FLOPs (floating-point operations), 61,000× larger message
